title: The realm of truth
hook: Sach Khand is described as the home of the Formless, the goal of the path
tomorrow: The five realms as a path

segments.voice: Yesterday, jivan mukat: free while living, where joy and sorrow weigh the same. Your line was free now. When something went wrong, could you take one breath before reacting? Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

Near the end of Japji, the morning prayer, Guru Nanak describes a series of realms, khands, like rooms opening one into the next. Tomorrow we'll walk the whole series. Today we go straight to the last room. And here's what's strange: when Guru Nanak gets there, after stanza upon stanza of description, he stops and admits something. Describing this place, he says, is hard. Hard like iron. The poet who has been naming worlds upon worlds reaches the realm of truth and tells you plainly that words strain here. Today's lesson is that room, and that honest admission.
screen: `REALMS, LIKE ROOMS.` → `STRAIGHT TO THE LAST ONE.` → `HARD LIKE IRON TO DESCRIBE.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Sach Khand: sach is truth, and khand is a realm, a region. The realm of truth. Who lives there? Japji says, in paraphrase: in the realm of truth dwells the Formless One, Nirankar. Creating, the One watches over the creation, and blesses it with the glance of grace. The same glance, nadar, we met with the robe and the door. Here it isn't a single look at a single person. It's the One gazing on everything made, with joy. What's in it? The pauri says there are worlds there, and continents, and universes, beyond counting, and if anyone tried to count them, there would be no end. Form upon form, and all of them moving as the hukam moves them. The One sees them and is glad. Here the threads of this week come together: the order everything lives within, the grace that opens the door, the Formless One who is beyond and within. Sach Khand is where they meet. Then the honest end. Guru Nanak closes the description, in paraphrase: to describe this, Nanak says, is as hard as iron. Sikh readers take Sach Khand as the goal of the path, the home of the Formless. Some read it as a place the soul reaches; some as a state of union lived even now, which links it back to yesterday's free while living. The text holds the door open, and then admits it can't fully describe the room. Home in truth.
screen: `SACH KHAND: THE REALM OF TRUTH.` · `HOME OF THE FORMLESS.` · `WORLDS BEYOND COUNTING, IN THE HUKAM.` · `HARD AS IRON TO DESCRIBE.` · then, large: `HOME IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in truth. Settle, and breathe. Let go of trying to describe anything. Let the words in your head slow down, the way the Guru's words slowed at the edge of this realm. When a thought comes, notice it and let it pass without naming it. If you pray, you can rest in the sense of being seen by a gracious glance. If you don't, just rest in what's true right now: this breath, this room, this moment. Nothing to add. The bell holds the time.
The realm of truth. Sach Khand, which Japji calls the home of the Formless One, where creation is watched with grace, and which Guru Nanak says is as hard as iron to describe. Today's word.
Your line: home in truth. Today, say one thing that's simply true, without dressing it up, and notice how it feels to stand on it. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

fork.setup: you're a poet who has described realm after realm, and now you reach the last one, the realm of truth. what do you do?
options: describe it as confidently as all the others.
describe what you can, then admit words strain here.
skip it and end the poem early.
fork.reveal: Guru Nanak describes the Formless One's home, then says describing it is as hard as iron.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Sach Khand, the realm of truth, the home of the Formless.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sach Khand is the Sikh name for heaven, a reward after death.
what it means: the realm of truth, home of the Formless One, the goal of the path.
what a scholar hears: Japji's last realm ends with honesty: to describe it, Nanak says, is as hard as iron.
